paras: The lynching of Ofrio Baca was the hanging of a prisoner accused of murdering A. M. Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, by vigilantes at Socorro, New Mexico Territory, at the end of March 1881. Brought to Socorro under arrest from Mexico, he was taken from the jail and hanged from the gate of the courthouse yard. The territorial press reported the killing as Conklin's murder "revenged," and its gallows headline became a joke in eastern papers.

Conklin was killed at Socorro on Christmas evening of 1880. In late February 1881 a special from Socorro reported that "the two murderers of Conklin," named as Abran and Mesias Baca, had been arrested at Ysleta, Texas, by Texas Rangers, and that they denied being the right men. A Santa Fe dispatch carried the same news with the prediction that the two "will probably be lynched before arriving at Socorro."

According to the Las Vegas Gazette, Ofrio Baca, described as "the principal in the murder," was captured by Texas Rangers in old Mexico, who took him "without warrant" and brought him across the border. He was held at San Marcial until night, and his wife met him there in what the paper called a "very affecting" meeting. About twenty of his friends from Socorro also went down to San Marcial, but they were put off the caboose on the return trip for lack of fare.

Baca arrived at Socorro on a freight train near midnight and was taken to the jail. The vigilantes then "gathered in force," took him, and hanged him from the crossbeams of the gate in the courthouse yard until he was dead. The Gazette, which had reported the capture on 31 March, printed the hanging on 1 April, so it probably took place in the last days of March.

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the vigilantes appears in the coverage. The prosecution of the Conklin murder continued: in June a "Baca, the murderer of A. M. Conklin," was reported indicted at Socorro. In November a jury acquitted "a Mexican named Haca [Baca]" charged with complicity in the murder, after which a Socorro mob that had come "ready with a noose" ordered the prosecutor, Frank Chavez, out of town. Conklin's widow later published a card denying that she had been bribed to stay away from that trial.

The Las Vegas Gazette carried the fullest account under the headline "Conkling's Murder Revenged," treating Baca's guilt as settled while dwelling on his parting from his wife. Another territorial paper, the New Mexican News, headed its report "Hellward by Hemp," a phrase the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier repeated in a humor column on 14 April and the Willimantic Journal reprinted a week later. Outside the territory the hanging otherwise drew a single line in the Memphis Daily Appeal on 21 April, filed among Texas items and stating flatly that Bacca "murdered" Conkling. The February arrest dispatch, with its forecast of a lynching, had run more widely, in Chicago, Cheyenne and Lancaster papers. None of the reports mentions the race of the man hanged.

The Memphis Appeal placed the hanging at "Socorro, Texas," while the New Mexico reports and the Santa Fe wire place Socorro in New Mexico. The papers also do not reconcile the man hanged in March with the two Bacas named in February or with the Baca indicted and tried later in 1881 for the same murder.

bases: Vigilantes took Baca, held in the Socorro jail on the accusation of murdering editor Conklin, and hanged him from the courthouse yard gate (A5, A7).

Baca was hanged 'until he was dead' by 'the vigilantes' who 'gathered in force' at the jail, a group acting without legal authority (A5), called 'a Socorro mob' by the New Mexican News (A6); the pretext was punishment for the alleged murder of Conklin, under the headline 'Conkling's Murder Revenged' (A5).

The Las Vegas Gazette's account (A5) and the New Mexican News headline quoted in New Haven (A6) independently report the mob hanging of an alleged Conklin assassin at Socorro; the Memphis item (A7) appears to derive from the Gazette wording, and later reports of a living 'Baca' indicted and tried for the murder (A9, A10, A11) concern the case but do not deny the hanging.

framing.detail: The Las Vegas Gazette headed the report 'Conkling's Murder Revenged' and called Baca 'the principal in the murder', while describing his wife's 'very affecting' farewell.
The New Mexican News headline 'Hellward by Hemp' became a joke about headline style in the New Haven and Willimantic papers.
The Memphis Appeal stated as fact that Bacca 'murdered' Conkling and placed Socorro in Texas, in a column of Texas items.

info: Not stated; the Gazette of 1 April 1881 reported the hanging after giving news of the capture 'yesterday morning' (31 March), so about the last days of March 1881 (inferred); Memphis said 'a few days since' on 21 April.
Crossbeams of the gate in the court house yard, Socorro; Baca had first been taken to the jail.
Accused as 'the principal in the murder of A. M. Conklin editor of the Socorro Sun'; Conklin was killed at Socorro 'last Christmas evening' [December 1880].
'The vigilantes' (Gazette, Memphis); 'a Socorro mob' (New Mexican News via New Haven); no names.

Later in 1881 a living 'Baca' was indicted for Conklin's murder (June) and a 'Mexican named Haca [Baca]' charged with complicity was acquitted at Socorro (November); the papers do not reconcile him with the man hanged.
